extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, peer review researchers, medical researchers and reviewers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for moving from closed (anonymous) peer review toward open peer review in biomedical journals, including disclosure of reviewer identities and publication/visibility of review processes. Focuses on ethical, practical, and evidence-based considerations for designing peer review systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of reviewer identities to authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify to authors the names of those who have reviewed their papers, including in-house editorial and statistical advisers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BMJ will identify to authors the names of reviewers for all new papers; this is presented as an initial step toward openness and is supported on ethical grounds. Note: reviewers may decline to review if they do not want their identity revealed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full public openness of the peer review process
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the whole peer review process visible to anybody (e.g., on the World Wide Web), including publishing reviews and allowing readers to watch and contribute comments as the process occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editorial suggests moving beyond merely identifying reviewers to listing reviewers at the end of articles and making the review discourse public so peer review becomes a scientific discourse rather than a secret summary judgment. This aims to show added value and preserve journals' role in an electronic world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical obligation for openness
rubrics_metrics.description: It is ethically questionable for someone to pass judgment in secret; openness links privilege and duty and reminds reviewers that power carries responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary argument against closed review: secret judgments resemble totalitarian secrecy; naming reviewers is thought to reduce arbitrary or abusive judgments and encourage constructive criticism (quoting Drummond Rennie).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability and provision of academic credit
rubrics_metrics.description: Openness links accountability with credit, allowing reviewers to receive recognition for their reviewing work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By identifying reviewers, journals can give academic credit to reviewers (a defect of closed review is that reviewers receive no academic credit). This is presented as a benefit of open review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction of abusive or unethical reviewer behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Openness should reduce curt, abusive, destructive reviews and abuses such as idea theft and procrastination that occur under anonymity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors have observed abusive reviews that likely would not have been written if reviewers were identifiable. Openness is expected to eliminate some of the worst abuses where reviewers—under anonymity—steal ideas or otherwise misuse power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk to junior reviewers and potential loss of best reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Open review may deter junior reviewers from criticizing senior researchers for fear of reprisals, potentially excluding reviewers who provide the best opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editorial notes this 'sad' argument: junior reviewers (particularly those whose livelihoods depend on grants) may be reluctant; reviewers under 40 have been shown to give the best opinions. Journals must weigh this deterrent effect when adopting openness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary participation and right to decline
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should be allowed to decline to review a particular paper if they do not wish to be identified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BMJ states that a few reviewers have said they won't review if identified, and anyone can decline; this is part of a pragmatic implementation that respects reviewers' choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence-based evaluation of peer review practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes to peer review policy should be grounded in empirical research about their effects on review quality and recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites randomized trials: one small trial suggested blinding improves opinions, but two larger trials failed to find benefit; a BMJ trial found open review does not improve or worsen quality of opinions. The editorial argues for researching as changes are implemented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of peer review limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that peer review is slow, expensive, subjective, prone to bias, can be abused, poor at detecting gross defects, and almost useless at detecting fraud; its main benefit may be improving published work rather than perfect selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This diagnostic list frames realistic expectations for any peer review system and motivates reforms; evidence and literature (Lock, JAMA special issues) are cited to support these claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing ethical benefits against practical harms
rubrics_metrics.description: Weigh ethical arguments for openness (accountability, credit, reduced abuse) against practical harms (loss of candid junior reviewers, possible reduction in reviewer pool).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BMJ concludes the ethical reasons justify introducing open review despite risks, and will monitor effects—policy decisions should consider trade-offs and local context (e.g., authors' preferences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural change as a goal
rubrics_metrics.description: Use policy changes to encourage a broader culture change so junior researchers cease to fear reprisals from seniors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BMJ hopes small moves (identifying reviewers) will contribute to long-term cultural shifts that mitigate the deterrent effect on junior reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incremental implementation and ongoing research
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce openness gradually (first identifying reviewers to authors, then listing reviewers in articles, then full web-based transparency) while researching effects as changes proceed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BMJ describes a stepwise plan and emphasizes researching 'as we go' so that policy is informed by emerging evidence (e.g., randomized trials of blinding vs open review).
